output.proposed: Valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy — hold valproate in cirrhosis
interactions: Valproate inhibits carbamyl phosphate synthase I (CPSI) — the first enzyme in the urea cycle; raises ammonia even in patients without liver disease

Valproate is hepatotoxic in pre-existing liver disease — risk of worsening hepatic failure
contraindications: Valproate in hepatic encephalopathy — contraindicated; worsens hyperammonemia by direct urea cycle inhibition
Valproate in significant liver disease — relative/absolute contraindication depending on severity
warnings: Valproate withdrawal in bipolar disorder — risk of mood episode; must involve psychiatry
Alternative mood stabilizers without hepatotoxicity: lamotrigine (not hepatotoxic), lithium (if level corrected)

results.title: Mood stabilizer selection in hepatic impairment
results.summary: Valproate is contraindicated or should be used with extreme caution in hepatic impairment — causes dose-dependent hyperammonemia via urea cycle inhibition and is hepatotoxic. Lithium is renally eliminated and safe in liver disease but requires careful monitoring (thiazide diuretics increase levels). Lamotrigine is the preferred alternative mood stabilizer in hepatic impairment — primarily renally eliminated, no hepatotoxicity. Lamotrigine requires slow titration to avoid Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

output.summary: In patients with hepatic impairment, valproate is associated with dose-dependent hyperammonemia via urea cycle inhibition and carries hepatotoxic risk; published case series and pharmacokinetic studies support cautious use or avoidance. Lithium is renally eliminated and its clearance is reduced by thiazide diuretics, a well-documented interaction associated with toxicity. Lamotrigine has a renal elimination pathway and lacks known hepatotoxic effects in the published literature.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Hepatic encephalopathy with multifactorial hyperammonemia in alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 12) — driven by (1) valproate-induced urea-cycle inhibition (level 118 µg/mL), (2) lithium toxicity (1.6 mEq/L, HCTZ interaction), (3) quetiapine CNS depression, and (4) recent alcohol use.

differential.key_features: Lithium therapy + bipolar history; mania can mimic HE behavioral features but does not cause asterixis or respond to lactulose.
Level 1.6 mEq/L mildly toxic; tremor, confusion fit; HCTZ-lithium interaction is the trigger; treat with hydration and hold lithium.
Valproate inhibits urea-cycle carbamoyl phosphate synthase; can produce hyperammonemic encephalopathy independent of liver function; in a cirrhotic the effect amplifies.
Ethanol 22 mg/dL on arrival; monitor CIWA.
Empiric thiamine before dextrose given chronic alcohol.

optimal_actions.action: Send targeted laboratory studies: CBC, CMP, ammonia, magnesium, valproate_level, lactate, coagulation. Confirms liver dysfunction and screens for precipitants.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ammonia, valproate level (118 µg/mL), lithium level (1.6), ethanol 22, cirrhosis features.

optimal_actions.action: Non-contrast CT head — exclude structural alternate cause of AMS (hemorrhage, large stroke, mass) before any LP.
Literature/guideline search to confirm West Haven grading, precipitant management, and lactulose/rifaximin dosing (Valproate-induced hyperammonemia; lithium toxicity; HE in psychiatric polypharmacy).
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AASLD/EASL 2014 guidance retrieved; West Haven criteria and precipitant-driven management framework confirmed.

optimal_actions.action: Drug-interaction and medication-reconciliation review covering valproate (HOLD), lithium (HOLD), quetiapine (HOLD), HCTZ-lithium interaction, lactulose, rifaximin; substitute carnitine if valproate hyperammonemia confirmed; flag any CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, sedating antiemetics, antihistamines) and confirm lactulose/rifaximin dosing in liver disease.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sedating/CNS-depressant medications identified; lactulose and rifaximin reviewed for hepatic dose adjustment.

optimal_actions.action: EEG — exclude NCSE (especially valproate-related) and characterize encephalopathy. Triphasic waves are classic but non-specific (metabolic encephalopathies broadly); main role is exclusion of non-convulsive status epilepticus where the differential supports it.
Consult hepatology + psychiatry for bipolar regimen reformulation — coordinate definitive care, transplant candidacy assessment where applicable.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Hepatology / critical-care guidance integrated into management.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

sequence_constraints.reason: In altered mental status, exclude intracranial mass effect / hemorrhage on imaging before LP to avoid herniation risk.

critical_actions: Hold valproate and lithium immediately; check repeat levels.
IV L-carnitine 100 mg/kg if valproate-induced hyperammonemia is confirmed.
Hydrate (normal saline) to support lithium clearance; consider hemodialysis if lithium >2.5 with severe symptoms or AKI.
Lactulose 30 mL TID; rifaximin 550 mg BID.
Psychiatry to plan non-hepatotoxic bipolar regimen (e.g., lamotrigine).
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe benzodiazepines for anxiety/agitation — they precipitate and prolong HE (use haloperidol or non-pharmacologic measures for agitation).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids — they worsen HE; consider acetaminophen at hepatic-safe dosing for pain.
Do not perform LP before neuroimaging excludes mass effect when the patient has altered mental status.
Do not restart valproate in cirrhotic without strong indication — repeat hyperammonemia risk.
Avoid HCTZ-lithium combinations — well-known interaction that precipitated this toxicity.
key_reasoning_points: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grading + evidence of liver dysfunction + exclusion of other causes of AMS — ammonia level is supportive only and correlates poorly with grade (AASLD 2014).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Valproate can produce hyperammonemic encephalopathy in patients without overt liver disease (urea-cycle inhibition); in cirrhotics the effect is potentiated. L-carnitine reverses it.
Thiazides reduce lithium clearance; the lithium-HCTZ combination is a well-known cause of toxicity.
